blocks.title: DAY 7 — hospitals and restarting the grid
POWER BACK — the fridge (the payoff promised at 0:12)

captions.text: Your tap still runs when the power dies.
But why does it stop after about twenty-four hours...
and what do you lose first?
This is a what-if.
Most blackouts end in hours.
This one doesn't.
We're going to follow it for seven days...
hour by hour...
using the rules from the CDC, FEMA and the USDA.
And stay to the end.
Because the most dangerous moment isn't when the lights go out.
It's when they come back on...
and you open the fridge.
Hour one. Your lights go out.
That's the part everyone expects.
What comes next...
is what nobody does.
Your card stops working.
Card readers and ATMs need power and a network.
So it's cash only.
Then the gas station.
Here's the part that surprises people.
The station isn't out of gas.
The tanks under the ground are full.
But the only thing that lifts that fuel to your car is an electric pump.
No power... no pump.
A few states plan for this.
Florida, for example, requires many stations near highways and evacuation routes to be wired for a generator.
Most of the country has no rule like that.
And your fridge?
It starts a countdown.
Hour six. Your fridge just passed its four-hour mark.
The USDA rule: food in a closed fridge stays safe for about four hours.
After that, meat, milk, eggs and leftovers have to go.
Your freezer is your best friend now.
A full one holds for about forty-eight hours.
Half full? Just twenty-four.
Every traffic light is dark.
Many states write it into law: a dead signal means an all-way stop.
And your phone still has signal...
for now. Here's why that won't last.
A cell tower looks like a pole.
It's really a small building...
with a room full of batteries at the bottom.
Industry guidelines have called for as little as four hours of backup, with eight as the goal.
After Hurricane Katrina, the FCC tried to require eight hours nationwide.
That rule never took effect.
So the towers are draining.
And so is something you can't see.
Hour twelve. Your phone is at forty percent...
and it's dropping fast.
Your Wi-Fi router died the moment the power did.
So your phone leans on the cell network.
But the towers are weaker now.
As the signal drops, your phone works harder to stay connected...
and that burns battery.
And everyone is calling at once.
The network jams.
The FCC's advice: keep calls short, and text instead.
A text can get through when a call can't.
You can charge your phone in your car.
But only with the car outside, in the open.
Never in the garage.
Hold that thought...
it matters on day two.
But by hour twenty-four...
the problem isn't your phone.
It's your water.
Hour twenty-four.
So why did your tap keep running all this time?
Follow the pipe under your street.
It climbs a hill...
to a tank on legs.
A water tower.
The water up there is heavy.
Its own weight pushes it through every pipe in town.
That's your water pressure.
No motor. Just gravity.
Unless you live up high.
Many tall buildings use electric pumps to push water to the upper floors.
Up there, the tap can quit in the first hour.
But something had to lift that water up there.
Electric pumps.
And they stopped when the lights did.
Many systems are built to hold about one day of normal use up high.
So turn on your tap...
and listen. As the tower drains, the pressure drops.
And pressure is what keeps the pipes clean.
When it falls, dirty water can seep in through tiny cracks.
That's when a boil-water notice goes out.
The CDC's rule: a rolling boil for one full minute.
This is why the first thing to do in a blackout...
is fill everything.
Pots. Bottles.
The bathtub. Ready.gov says one gallon per person, per day.
And at hour forty-eight...
the real danger isn't hunger.
Hour forty-eight.
Even a full freezer is giving up now.
So people start cooking however they can.
Grills. Camp stoves.
Generators. And this is where blackouts turn deadly.
Carbon monoxide has no smell...
and no color. It doesn't make you cough.
The first signs are a headache...
dizziness... feeling tired.
In the dark, on day two, that feels normal.
So people lie down.
And the garage isn't the safe spot people think it is.
The CDC says don't even run a car in an attached garage...
with the door open.
The CDC counts more than four hundred deaths a year in the US from carbon monoxide that has nothing to do with fires.
The rule: never run a generator, a grill or a camp stove inside your home, your garage, or near a window.
Keep a generator at least twenty feet from doors and windows.
And a battery-powered CO alarm is the only thing that will warn you.
And at hour seventy-two...
the cold moves in.
